item.title: Fact-Checking Stephen Miller, the New White House Chief of Staff
item.description:
In ascending to the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, a longtime aide and hard-liner, has displayed messaging that mirrors that of President Trump: bombastic, combative and, at times, unabashedly fact-free.

Mr. Miller, who previously served as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, has promoted some of the second Trump administration’s most egregious falsehoods about immigration policy, the economy and political opposition. His loyalty to Mr. Trump was on show at the president’s news conference on Friday, where he lauded Mr. Trump as having achieved “more than any president has achieved by far in American history,” ticking off a list of the administration’s accomplishments.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, praised Mr. Miller in a statement. “Any good chief of staff reflects the messaging of the president they serve, who was elected by the American people,” she said.

In January, during the administration’s immigration surge in Minnesota, Mr. Miller swiftly called Alex Pretti, the nurse fatally shot by immigration officials, a “domestic terrorist” and accused him of trying to “murder” federal agents — a description at odds with legal reality and video evidence. This summer, Mr. Miller insisted that gas prices had been tamed and inflation had decreased to 2 percent — average gas prices neared $4.20 in August and inflation had risen by 3.4 percent in July. And as the midterm elections neared, Mr. Miller repeatedly and falsely characterized a Democratic Senate candidate as transgender.

Here are four other claims from Mr. Miller, fact-checked.

What Mr. Miller Said

“Let’s go back in history. How do we end up with 60 senators in the first place in 2008 to pass Obamacare? Because Democrats rigged the Alaska election then with a fake case against then-Senator Ted Stevens. So there is a history here where Alaska Democrats have tried corruptly to steal the vote of the Alaskan people and their right to choose their own future.”— in a Fox News interview in October

This is misleading. Senator Ted Stevens, Republican of Alaska, was prosecuted and convicted of corruption in October 2008 by the Justice Department under President George W. Bush. The conviction was thrown out the next year and the case was reviewed and dropped by the Obama administration in 2009. While the Alaska Democratic Party and Senator Mark Begich, Mr. Stevens’s Democratic challenger, attacked Mr. Stevens with accusations of corruption, they were not involved in the handling of the case.

Mr. Stevens was voted out of office in the face of a wide-ranging corruption investigation involving an oil company and its ties to lawmakers in Alaska opened by the Justice Department under Mr. Bush. Federal authorities searched the office of Mr. Stevens’s son, a state legislator, in 2006 and searched Mr. Stevens’s home in 2007. The senator was charged on seven felony counts in July 2008 for failing to disclose gifts from the company and its executive.

That executive, who tended to support Republican candidates, began cooperating with the authorities in the investigation in 2006 and was a key witness in the case against Mr. Stevens. The senator was convicted in October 2008 and lost his re-election bid the next month.

Three months later, in February 2009, an F.B.I. whistle-blower accused prosecutors of concealing evidence from the court and defense lawyers. The Justice Department, under the Obama administration, dropped its case against Mr. Stevens in April and Mr. Stevens’s lawyer said he was “very grateful” to Eric H. Holder Jr., the attorney general, for the decision.

The department and a special investigator appointed by a court released separate reviews of the case in 2012, two years after Mr. Stevens died in a plane crash. Both faulted prosecutors for misconduct and mistakes, but neither attributed those errors to political or partisan motivations. The special investigator told Congress that year that he believed the prosecutors’ desire to win a big case, compounded by tight deadlines, led to the misconduct.

What Mr. Miller Said

“First is we get off of this ridiculous path of having our children get 70 to 90 shots. That is wantonly excessive. Remember, each and every one of these shots produces a profound immunological response. So across any large population, if you give a kid shot after shot after shot, you’re going to have vaccine injuries, you’re going to have immunological issues, you’re going to have potentially neurological issues. Secondly, and so important to you, Mr. President, is the unbundling of the shot. Why do you need to have these shots bundled into these packages? Why can’t you split it into five visits and give this young body, if a parent wants to do a vaccine, one shot at a time? Why is it that in Japan you can get a separate measles shot, a separate mumps shot, a separate rubella shot, but in America it has to all be packaged together?”— in an executive order signing at the White House in August

This is misleading. Mr. Miller overstated the number of vaccines given to American children and offered a contradictory critique of the United States’ vaccine schedule.

The federal government in January tried to reduce the number of recommended vaccines for children to 11 diseases, from 17, but that effort is pending litigation. (In August, Mr. Trump signed an executive order trying the same thing, but it is unclear whether the order has any legal power.)

If children received every recommended dose from birth until they were 18, they would receive 72 doses. That is different from 72 different shots or 72 different vaccines. Annual flu and coronavirus vaccines constitute about half of those doses. (Fewer than half of children obtained a flu vaccine last year, and fewer than 10 percent received a coronavirus shot.) Other vaccines, like hepatitis B and polio, are given in multiple doses. And some vaccines like diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis as well as measles, mumps and rubella are given together.

Japan does offer separate vaccines for mumps, measles and rubella. But it is an outlier, especially among peer nations. In fact, most countries — including the United States, Canada and most European nations — use the combined trivalent shot. Just 15 countries, all low- and middle-income countries in Africa and the Middle East, used a monovalent measles shot. Moreover, Mr. Miller’s suggestion to separate all three vaccines would lead to more shots, not fewer — conflicting with his critique of a high number of doses. Health experts recommend the combined shot for logistical ease and to encourage higher vaccination levels.

What Mr. Miller Said

“So, when you think about, for example, public schools, half of kids in New York public schools can’t speak English properly. Why? Because 40 percent of New York City public or New York State school students are either migrants or the children of migrants. They’re redistributing education from the taxpaying base to newcomers.”— in a Fox News interview in August

This is misleading. Mr. Miller appears to be exaggerating and conflating several different statistics to suggest that New York City schools show how immigrants are taking resources from native-born Americans.

Under a 1982 Supreme Court ruling, public schools cannot bar students from attending based on citizenship, so they generally do not track immigration status. But the Center for Immigration Studies, a research group that supports lower levels of immigration, has estimated, using Census Bureau data, that 47 percent of public school students in the New York City metropolitan area lived in households headed by an immigrant.

A smaller proportion of students, though, “can’t speak English properly,” as Mr. Miller said. About 15.4 percent of students in New York schools were English-language learners in the 2025-26 school year, according to the city. But that does not necessarily mean they were immigrants. Census surveys estimate that some 1.5 million New Yorkers who are native-born citizens and 1.4 million naturalized citizens speak a language other than English at home.

Mr. Miller does have a point that most research shows that immigrant households cost local governments more money than they pay in local taxes. While immigrants have a net positive fiscal effect on the federal budget, they generally have a net negative effect on local and state governments given the cost of education. But that does not mean native-born Americans are being pushed out of public schools; rather, enrollment at New York City schools is declining, fueled by a two-decade decrease in fertility rates and mirroring a trend seen across the country.

What Mr. Miller Said

“The way most welfare works in most states, and most places, is we take your word for it. If you fill out a piece of paper and you say your kids are hungry, you are going to get food stamps. We don’t check as a country if you even have kids.”— at a meeting of the White House fraud task force in May

False. Applicants to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps, undergo eligibility interviews and give proof of identity, residency, income and assets, expenses and other details listed on the application. State agencies must also recertify most SNAP participants every year. (There are exceptions for some low-income seniors in some states, who are recertified every three years.)

Applicants must list the date of birth and Social Security number of each household member and, contrary to Mr. Miller’s claim, state SNAP agencies then verify this information with the Social Security Administration. Similarly, agencies and workers rely on a variety of government databases and private companies to check residency, immigration status, income, assets, disability status and employment history.

The Government Accountability Office, in a 2024 review of the SNAP program, found that about 11.7 percent of payments in the 2023 fiscal year were improper (which is not the same thing as fraud), stemming from a variety of errors including state agencies’ not always verifying household size. The watchdog office did not estimate how widespread that oversight was.

item.title: ‘I Said a Little Prayer’: A Riverboat Captain Recalls a Crash on the Mississippi
item.description:
Capt. Len Stewart was wrapping up paperwork in his pilothouse on Nov. 13 atop the American Heritage, a riverboat docked in New Orleans, when a loud blast from a horn interrupted his focus.

He saw a tanker on the Mississippi River hurtling toward him and the nearly 200 passengers who were mingling across his ship’s five decks. Captain Stewart, 51, had just finished an eight-day riverboat tour, a trip he estimated he had completed more than 30 times.

Someone aboard the 525-foot tanker repeatedly sounded the horn to signal trouble, leaving Captain Stewart about 20 seconds to prepare those aboard for impact, he said.

He raced through the ship, alerting as many people as he could, when he reached the fourth floor. He braced himself on a stairwell and heard a crunch as the tanker crashed into the American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m.

The next few hours were filled with the harrowing moments of Captain Stewart and crew members working to save lives. Thirty-two people were hospitalized, and two people had serious injuries.

Ultimately, though, everyone aboard survived through the efforts of rescuers, firefighters, police officers and volunteers.

“Every time I tell the story, it’s emotional for me,” Captain Stewart said. “I don’t want to relive that again.”

In a phone interview on Friday, Captain Stewart, of Mobile, Ala., spoke about his experience during an averted tragedy that the New Orleans mayor called the “Miracle on the Mississippi.” These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

How did you become interested in becoming a riverboat captain?

A friend who was a captain convinced me to switch careers in my 20s. I used to manage fine-dining restaurants.

What did you see before the crash?

I had about 20 seconds before the ship hit us. I took about five of them to make a quick announcement telling everybody to brace for impact. Then we sprinted to the stern of the vessel, banging on doors along the way.

We went down one level to the fourth deck, which is an outdoor seating area. I told everybody to get away from the side, get down, brace for impact.

And then, bam! It was like a bomb went off. All the pilings that were tied under the dock all exploded into wooden shrapnel.

The boat was sliding away from the dock. So I made mayday calls, begging for help, telling everybody we’re taking on water. We need immediate assistance. We have 200 people on board, a lot of elderly people. We need help.

Our bow was probably 30 feet off the dock. If we didn’t get back into the dock, nobody was getting off the boat. Less than two minutes later, this tug pulled up. He just shoved us in. The people on the dock were able to pull it up and get the gangway situated so we could start getting people off.

Your crew is trying to usher people off the boat, but it begins taking on a lot of water. It’s going to tilt and potentially capsize.

I was like, oh my God. This thing is about to flip over. The boat starts pitching, and I knew once it pitched, there’s no coming back. I don’t have any way to make any announcements. I thought for sure people were going to die.

The boat flipped, and I slid down 50 feet into the deck boxes, basically a straight drop. I tried to brace myself as much as possible with my legs, and then I slammed into the handrail and rolled into the water.

What were you thinking at that moment?

I said a little prayer: God, please protect me. Luckily, the fire and rescue boat was right there. They picked me up in three or four minutes. I grabbed a pike pole and started to help fish people out of the water. We’d bend down and grab their life jacket and belt loops, and yank them onto the boat. I stayed on that vessel until the last person was out of the water.

After you conducted these rescues, you were taken to a command center, where officials worked to figure out how many people had survived and died. What do you remember?

When I got there, there were 33 people who were unaccounted for. Every 30 minutes, there would be an update, and the number kept getting smaller. When they said zero unaccounted for, everybody just started going crazy, clapping and screaming and yelling.

Anything else you’d like to add?

I appreciate all the accolades. Ultimately, I’m just doing my job. The real heroes are my crew, the first responders, the tugboat captains and the Good Samaritans. We had servers and housekeepers and hotel managers carrying people up the steps to get them outside the vessel, selfless crew members giving their life jackets to guests. They went above and beyond the call of duty. I have not had an outlet to say thank you yet. It was a team effort.

item.title: What’s Legal Under Florida’s New Anti-D.E.I. Law? It’s Anyone’s Guess.
item.description:
A Florida law set to take effect in January prompted officials in Delray Beach this month to pre-emptively cancel the city’s St. Patrick’s Day parade, drawing national headlines and outrage across the political divide.

The decision was but one example of how governments and cultural organizations across the state are hustling to comply with the law, which Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, signed in the spring as part of a broader crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion activities. But Republican lawmakers and Mr. DeSantis, who likes to say Florida is “where woke goes to die,” may not have expected quite this much upheaval.

In the Florida Keys, officials have cut grants for Pride events, drag shows and an Italian heritage organization, while a decades-old women’s flag football tournament added a men’s division to keep its public funding. Broward County can’t fund a Greek film festival, a boy’s choir or a women’s tennis tournament, according to one commissioner, citing legal advice from the county attorney’s office.

Officials in Fernandina Beach, near Jacksonville, issued a proclamation celebrating a Hispanic heritage festival, only to learn minutes later from the town attorney that doing so will be illegal next year.

The law bans local governments from directly or indirectly funding, promoting, or taking official action related to D.E.I.-related activities. And it defines D.E.I. as anything promoting or providing preferential treatment or special benefits based on “race, color, sex, ethnicity, gender identity, or sexual orientation.”

Mr. DeSantis called Delray Beach’s parade cancellation “malicious compliance” aimed at scoring political points; the city’s mayor told The South Florida Sun-Sentinel that its legal department deemed the parade an “ethnic” event that promotes a certain group.

Critics say the law has enough ambiguities that local officials are erring on the side of caution to avoid its penalties: It allows residents to sue if they think their city or county is violating the law, or the governor to remove officials who violate it.

“The ambiguity of the law is already having a chilling effect,” said Jon Harris Maurer, general counsel for Equality Florida, an L.G.B.T.Q. rights group that opposes the law.

Mr. DeSantis, who leaves office in January because of term limits, has molded Florida into a conservative bastion, making his “war on woke” a top priority. During his tenure, Florida has restricted public school lessons on gender and sexuality, overhauled standards on teaching African-American history, and cracked down on rainbow art on crosswalks. More than a dozen Republican-led states have passed anti-D.E.I. laws, typically centered on educational issues.

Mr. DeSantis, speaking after Republicans were drubbed nationally in the November midterm elections but retained power in Florida, said the state “took care” of addressing so-called woke overreach while acknowledging many voters now have different concerns. His office did not respond to a request for comment.

Florida’s Republican-dominated Legislature passed the anti-D.E.I. law in part to restrict cities’ and counties’ spending on diversity training. Dean Black, a Republican state representative, said at the time that such efforts “fostered resentment instead of good will, mediocrity instead of merit, and divided our society against itself.”

The law does not prevent local governments from recognizing or promoting federal holidays, or groups honored by monuments, memorial and museums that have been authorized by Florida law. That allowed Delray Beach to keep funding the Spady Cultural Heritage Museum, for example, which is dedicated to Black culture and history in Palm Beach County.

Yet a lawyer for the city concluded that continuing to fund its popular St. Patrick’s Day parade — which draws revelers and bagpipe players from around the nation — would create “meaningful legal risk.”

Alex Andrade, a former Republican state representative from Pensacola who voted for the bill, said that he thought some local governments were interpreting the law too broadly, though he acknowledged that “the language could be made sharper.”

Clay Yarborough, a Republican state senator who sponsored the bill, wrote on X that when the bill was being debated, “the specific question was asked related to whether St. Patricks Day observances would be prohibited. The answer was and still is no.”

Critics said such an interpretation amounts to an admission that white heritage celebrations meet the law’s guidelines, while those recognizing other ethnicities do not.

“It’s a slap in the face to feel that we are not worthy of support,” said Calibe Thompson, the executive director of Island SPACE Caribbean Museum in Plantation, Fla., which celebrates Caribbean culture in a county with a large population born on the islands.

In October, Broward County denied the museum a nearly $25,000 grant — a meaningful amount for an operation that runs on a shoestring budget, she said.

Across Florida, government lawyers and elected officials have been searching for legal footing to justify continuing longstanding support for some events.

Broward County Commissioner Steven Geller said that as a hypothetical, the county might get away with supporting an event on French cooking because it represents a style of cuisine, but not one that incorporates elements of French culture.

He said the county feels it must tread carefully. It is overwhelmingly Democratic, and state Republicans have previously criticized its diversity practices.

“We are an obvious target,” said Mr. Geller, a lawyer and Democrat who formerly served as the State Senate minority leader.

Some arts and cultural organizations in Broward are scaling back. Florida Singing Sons, a five-decade old boy’s choir, lost $45,000 in grants because of the law and plans to reduce performances. Other groups are rebranding or broadening their mission statements to keep public funding.

Miami has historically provided about $90,000 to sponsor the annual Gay8 Festival, an annual Latin L.G.B.T.Q. music, food, and arts event in the Little Havana neighborhood.

Now, the festival has refashioned itself as the 8 Freedom Festival, its website devoid of mentions of L.G.B.T.Q. advocacy. “We’re entering the realm of the theater of the absurd,” said Damian Pardo, the first openly gay city commissioner in Miami history, who helped found the event before he was elected.

Miami commissioners next month will consider an ordinance that would gut an L.G.B.T.Q. advisory board and other equal-opportunity programs.

While legal uncertainty reigns, organizations that have long counted on public funding are looking elsewhere.

An arts nonprofit in Delray Beach said Friday that it hopes to revive the nearly six-decade old St. Patrick’s Day Parade, in part with GoFundMe contributions.

In the Keys, county officials eliminated more than $200,000 in annual grants to the Key West Business Guild to market L.G.B.T.Q. events during the slow summer months. Also gone is a $4,800 monthly stipend to the Gay Key West Visitors Center, run by the guild, which paid its rent on the city’s famed Duval Street.

A newly formed nonprofit, Southernmost Alliance for Equality, is asking people to consider donating $19.78 per month to help pay the visitor center’s rent; the amount is a tribute to 1978, the year the business guild started. So far, it’s raised about $4,000.

“We still have a long way to go,” said Dustin Bass, the alliance’s president.

item.title: F.A.A. Says All Delta Flights Through Atlanta Delayed as Automated System Falters
item.description:
All Delta Air Lines flights traveling to and from Atlanta were delayed on Sunday morning after a problem was reported with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance, the Federal Aviation Administration said.

The disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Delta’s largest hub and one of the world’s busiest airports, come a week after a nationwide ground stop that resulted in the cancellation of thousands of flights. That was followed by a United Airlines problem on Monday that also caused delays.

“Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems,” the F.A.A. said in a statement on Sunday.

Flights have been delayed for about an hour.

All Delta flights departing to Atlanta from within the contiguous United States are affected, as are flights leaving Atlanta, according to the F.A.A. advisory. Delta is the only commercial airline subject to the delay program.

The airline’s departures started to underperform at 6 a.m., according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. By 7 a.m., 26 percent of Delta flights had been canceled or did not fly.

At Hartsfield-Jackson airport, more than 40 percent of Delta flights were delayed by 9 a.m., Cirium said.

The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.

“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.

The airline also said it was working with air traffic controllers to help alleviate congestion at their Atlanta hub.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

item.title: Democrats Clinch 258 House Seats, an Election-Year Record This Century
item.description:
Democrats on Sunday secured the largest House majority in a national election in three decades, capturing at least 258 seats in the chamber in a sweeping backlash to rising prices and President Trump’s tumultuous second term.

Election officials were still tallying votes, and a small group of races remained too close to call. But the latest race calls by The Associated Press showed that Democrats, notching victories that extended far into conservative corners of the country, had won more House seats than in any election since the early 1990s.

They eclipsed the 257 seats they won in the 2008 election, when Barack Obama thundered past Senator John McCain atop the ticket in a wave of Democratic enthusiasm and a backlash to the presidency of George W. Bush. (In 2009, Democrats briefly reached 258 seats after a special election win in New York.)

Democrats reached 258 seats on Sunday with a victory in North Carolina: Chuck Hubbard, a Democrat and a former newspaper reporter, defeated Representative Virginia Foxx, an 11-term Republican. The Associated Press called the race Sunday afternoon, after election officials completed a recount a day earlier.

Democrats captured 258 seats to Republicans’ 173. A handful of races remained unsettled.

Sources: Ballotpedia and The Associated Press.

Elena Shao/The New York Times

Neither party had won so many seats in a national election since 1992, when Democrats clinched 258 as Bill Clinton took the presidency. Republicans have not controlled more than 250 House seats since the Great Depression. The largest House majority on record was the 334 seats that Democrats commanded at the end of the 1930s.

This year, Democrats overcame a flurry of gerrymandering by Republican-led state legislatures that put the Republican Party at a structural advantage going into Election Day.

“The people of our great country delivered House Democrats a historic majority with a mandate to fight for an Affordable America,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader, who is on track to be the first Black speaker, said in a statement. “Together, we will work hard to deliver the dramatic change in direction the American people are demanding.”

Democrats had surprising wins all over the country, ousting Republicans from New York to Indiana to Arizona. Republican bright spots were rare. Nationally almost every congressional district shifted toward Democrats compared with 2024’s results. As of Sunday, Republicans had flipped just one House seat from Democratic control in a district that was not gerrymandered. (That seat was in Maine.)

The far-reaching gains for Democrats in the House mirrored their sweeping victories in the Senate, as voters voiced displeasure with inflation under Mr. Trump — who once vowed to “make America affordable again” — and his unpopular war in Iran.

Kevin McCarthy, the Republican former House speaker from California, said in an interview that Democrats had enjoyed a “generational” victory and that Republicans’ gerrymandering efforts had failed. In some cases, Mr. McCarthy added, the new district lines “probably played against us.”

Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, has said his party “left it all on the field” and ran on a message of “common sense,” accusing Democrats of having “Trump derangement syndrome.”

Mr. Johnson said after the election that he would not run to lead the House Republican conference next year. This month, House Republicans elected Representative Jim Jordan, a fiery Ohio lawmaker and close Trump ally, to replace Mr. Johnson as their leader once they are relegated to the minority next year.

House Democrats’ campaign arm, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in a memo dated Nov. 9 that the party’s midterm success was the result of its focus on the economy and rising prices. Democrats won 70 of the 92 House districts that the party considered battlegrounds, according to the memo.

Every Democrat who ran for re-election in a district redrawn by Republican cartographers emerged victorious, the memo said. Among those was Representative Don Davis of North Carolina, whose path in his gerrymandered district was once described as “incredibly difficult” by the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster. (Republicans did flip a seat in Tennessee, where Representative Steve Cohen decided not to run for re-election in his carved-up Memphis-area district. Republicans also flipped a Texas seat in the Dallas suburbs that Representative Julie Johnson chose not to defend after redistricting.)

Newt Gingrich, the Republican from Georgia who served as House speaker for four years after his party won landslide victories in the 1994 midterms, attributed this year’s wave to voters’ anger about gasoline costs that were driven up by the war.

“People decided that Republicans weren’t paying attention, they weren’t getting the job done,” Mr. Gingrich said in an interview, adding, “It liberates Hakeem to do almost what he wants, because he’s going to have enough votes on virtually everything.”

Democrats and Republicans have traded narrow majorities in recent years. Slim margins forced Mr. Johnson and his immediate predecessor, Mr. McCarthy — the California Republican who was speaker for most of 2023 — to negotiate with a small group of far-right members who sometimes had different priorities.

Mr. Jeffries is set to have “far more maneuvering room,” said Steve Israel, who was a New York representative from 2001 to 2017 and the chair of House Democrats’ campaign arm for much of the Obama administration.

“It’s like a night-and-day difference,” Mr. Israel said. He added, “If it was a three-vote majority, every single bill that the Democrats had to consider would require threading a needle and would have clearly elevated the far left.”

Mr. Trump will still be able to veto legislation passed by Democratic majorities in Congress, and he at times has vowed to aggressively wield his veto pen. “I’ll become Mr. Veto,” Mr. Trump told The New York Post days before the election, referring to the possibility of Democrats taking control of Congress, though the president has also at times signaled a willingness to work with Democrats since the Election Day drubbing.

Mr. McCarthy suggested that Mr. Jeffries would have less work and more power ahead of him than Mr. McCarthy had when he assumed the gavel in 2023. (It took Mr. McCarthy five days, 15 votes and countless failed negotiations with far-right Republicans to win the speakership after the 2022 midterms.)

“I would have loved it,” Mr. McCarthy chuckled, referring to the size of the incoming majority, adding that Mr. Jeffries would be able to allow members on different sides of issues to vote against bills without it sinking the legislation’s chances. “It gives real power.”

Mr. McCarthy marveled at the majority Democrats had secured.

“Back to the ’90s,” he said. “Jeez.”

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: Democrat Unseats 11-Term G.O.P. House Member in North Carolina
item.description:
Chuck Hubbard, a Democrat and a former newspaper reporter, unseated Representative Virginia Foxx of North Carolina on Sunday, according to The Associated Press, ousting an 11-term Republican who leads one of the House’s most powerful committees.

Mr. Hubbard’s victory, which expanded Democrats’ largest House majority in decades, was part of a nationwide electoral shift toward Democrats in the midterm elections. Mr. Hubbard defeated Ms. Foxx by about 300 votes in one of the country’s closest races.

Just two years ago, Mr. Hubbard lost to Ms. Foxx, 83, by nine percentage points. But this time, he outperformed her in some of the more populous counties of North Carolina’s Fifth Congressional District, which sprawls from the conservative northwestern part of the state into the Democratic-leaning area around Greensboro.

On Sunday, Ms. Foxx called Mr. Hubbard to concede, after a recount was completed a day earlier. Mr. Hubbard said in a statement that she had “graciously” congratulated him and added, “Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service.”

Ms. Foxx said in a statement that she had offered Mr. Hubbard her “best wishes as he represents this wonderful district.”

Mr. Hubbard, 64, a longtime reporter at the Wilkes Journal-Patriot, a weekly newspaper in North Wilkesboro, N.C., that his grandfather founded, focused his campaign on a message of economic populism: lowering costs for working families, reining in an administration often aligned with billionaires under President Trump and criticizing Ms. Foxx’s support for Mr. Trump and the billionaire Elon Musk.

“As a local journalist, I spent 40 years reporting the truth and holding those in power accountable,” Mr. Hubbard said in an ad he posted on social media last month, adding: “I’m running for Congress to lower costs, to stop the spread of data centers and to ban members of Congress from trading stocks.”

Mr. Hubbard received attention online after a TikTok video from last year, in which he said that protecting his gay daughter and other L.G.B.T.Q. people had inspired him to run for Congress, began circulating widely. He also posted videos of himself making cotton candy and dancing Zumba.

Mr. Hubbard ran unsuccessfully for North Carolina’s Statehouse in 2022 before losing to Ms. Foxx as a Democratic challenger two years later. Ms. Foxx was elected in 2004 and serves as the chairwoman of the House Rules Committee.

Mr. Hubbard led Ms. Foxx by 99 votes on election night, and the margin remained tight for an extended period as the race remained uncalled. He traveled to Washington to join freshman lawmakers in orientation last week, before the race was officially called.

Tim Balk contributed reporting.

item.title: A Father Who Crusaded Against Steroids in Sports Has Died
item.description:
By 2005, the use of performance-enhancing drugs had become rampant, with players adding 20 to 30 pounds of new muscle. Home runs were flying out of ballparks. Mark McGwire slammed a record 70 home runs in 1998 (while conceding that he had used a supplement that was a steroid precursor). Three years later, a bulked-up Barry Bonds hit 73.

It was all great business for Major League Baseball, as many more fans bought tickets and watched television to keep track of the steroids-fueled homer circus. The league’s officials seemed resistant to addressing the widespread use of illicit drugs.

Then, on March 17, 2005, in a Congressional hearing room, the tide turned.

The slippery testimony that day by some of baseball’s biggest stars — Mr. McGwire, Sammy Sosa and Rafael Palmeiro — only worsened baseball’s public-relations nightmare.

But it was the impassioned testimony from a lesser-known witness, Donald Hooton Sr., a grieving father from Texas, that resonated beyond baseball.

Mr. Hooton’s son Taylor, a high school pitcher, had hanged himself two years earlier, after several months of taking steroids that he hoped would make him bigger.

Mr. Hooton put some of the blame for his son’s and many other teenagers’ use of the drugs on professional athletes.

“Players that are guilty of taking steroids are not only cheaters — you are cowards!” Mr. Hooton told the House Committee on Government Reform, which was investigating the use of performance enhancing drugs in Major League Baseball.

“You’re afraid to step on the field to compete for your positions and play the game without the aid of substances that are a felony to possess without a legitimate prescription,” he said, “substances that have been banned from competition at all levels of athletics.”

He added, “What message are you sending our sons and daughters? That you’re above the law? That you can continue to deny your behavior and get away with it? That somehow you’re not a cheater unless you get caught?”

Another parent, Denise Garibaldi, also testified that day, about her son Rob, who died by suicide after using steroids.

A few days after the hearing, baseball’s commissioner, Bud Selig, called Mr. Hooton at his home in Plano, Texas. He told Mr. Hooton that he had been moved by his testimony.

“It broke my heart,” Mr. Selig told The New York Post in August 2005, when he announced that Major League Baseball would pay $1 million over two years to be a founding sponsor of the Taylor Hooton Foundation for Fighting Steroid Abuse. In all, M.L.B. has contributed $8.5 million to the foundation.

Mr. Hooton started the nonprofit in 2004 to educate young people, including athletes, as well as the adults who influence them, about the dangers of performance-enhancing drugs, including steroids, human growth hormone and dietary supplements.

The foundation’s small staff delivers some 200 programs a year at middle schools, high schools and colleges; at M.L.B. ballparks with the Professional Baseball Athletic Trainers Society, and to law enforcement officers who work at schools, according to Don Hooton Jr., Taylor’s older brother and the foundation’s president.

It also collaborates with Major League Baseball — players from its 30 teams sit on the foundation’s MLB advisory board — on public service announcements that appear in team programs. The Yankees have held 16 Give a Hoot Benefits in a suite at Yankee Stadium.

Under continuing Congressional pressure, baseball and the players’ union greatly stiffened its existing drug-testing program by increasing penalties for a failed steroid test to suspension for 50 games for a first violation, 100 games for a second and a lifetime ban for a third.

It brought some satisfaction to Mr. Hooton.

“No, I honestly didn’t think it would move that fast,” he told The Baltimore Sun after the drug-testing program was announced. “It’s a great step forward. I couldn’t be more pleased.”

Don Hooton Jr., said that his father was inspired to create the foundation by a line from Genesis: “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.”

Mr. Hooton died on Nov. 10 at his home in McKinney, Texas. He was 75.

Don Jr. said the cause was cancer.

Donald Milton Hooton was born on March 30, 1950, in Longview, Texas, and grew up mostly in Lafayette, La. His father, Claude, was an accountant for Exxon, and his mother, Mary Julia (Reinberger) Hooton, who managed the home, was a volunteer church bookkeeper before her marriage. One of Don’s cousins is Burt Hooton, who won 151 games with three M.L.B. teams in the 1970s and ’80s.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in business administration and economics from the University of Southwestern Louisiana (now the University of Louisiana at Lafayette) in 1972, Mr. Hooton began a sales and marketing career with telecommunications and technology companies, including Hewlett-Packard, where he was a director of worldwide marketing. He retired from corporate work to run the foundation.

A right-handed pitcher, Taylor was 16 when he began injecting himself with steroids in late 2002. A junior varsity coach had counseled him to get bigger and more muscular — Taylor stood 6-foot-1 and weighed 175 pounds — to better compete for a spot on the varsity team in his senior year. The coach didn’t tell him how to get bigger, but Taylor believed the best path was through steroids, which several of his teammates were using.

He soon developed telltale signs of steroid abuse: severe acne on his back; weight gain of about 30 pounds; puffiness in his face; and emotions including euphoria, aggression and depression.

Mr. Hooton said that he and his wife, Gwen, recognized the physical and emotional changes in Taylor but were unaware they could be related to steroid abuse.

While seeing a psychiatrist, Taylor confessed that he was using steroids and quit the drugs nearly two months before he died. But he fell into a depression that Mr. Hooton attributed to ending his use of steroids.

On July 15, 2003, when Taylor didn’t respond to his mother’s question about what he wanted for lunch, she found him hanging from a belt from his bedroom door.

When the police inspected Taylor’s room they discovered vials of steroids, as well as syringes and needles. An autopsy found the presence of two steroids in his system.

Mr. Hooton quickly delved into research to understand the connection between steroids and their side effects. “It was right there in black and white,” he recalled on a 2019 podcast on his foundation’s website.

Once he felt knowledgeable enough, he asked the principal of Taylor’s high school in Plano if he could speak to students and parents. In the school’s gymnasium less than two months after Taylor’s death, Mr. Hooton and a doctor addressed about 600 people in the gymnasium.

“Parents, I want you to imagine for a moment how horrifying it was to go through his room after the funeral and find his stash of needles and syringes,” Mr. Hooton said, according to The Dallas Morning News. “For some of you in this audience, this horrifying activity is going on in your homes right now.”

The article led to a whirlwind of media attention, which included a front-page report in The New York Times and a segment on CBS’s “60 Minutes II,” and invitations to testify to Congress.

In addition to Don Jr., and his wife, Gwen (Hopkins) Hooton, Mr. Hooton is survived by his daughter Mackenzie Hooton; four grandchildren, and his brothers James and Richard. In 2009, when Alex Rodriguez, then a Yankee, admitted that he had used steroids while playing for the Texas Rangers years earlier, Mr. Hooton said that news like Rodriguez’s was beneficial for his foundation.

“When it’s in the headlines, we get to talk to people,” he told The Kansas City Star. “As long it’s on the front pages, the public has some appetite for talking about this. As soon as it’s not on the front pages, nobody wants to talk about it anymore. It’s painful for the public, but this is reality.”
